scenes.title: The tide-book
scenes.text:
The ninth bell had already gone when Tamsin Vey climbed the back stair of the Customs House, and Assessor Mallory was waiting for her at the top of it with his watch open in his palm like an accusation.

"Low water at a quarter past," he said. "You know that. The whole city knows that. The gulls know that."

"The gulls don't have to come from the Narrows."

"The gulls," Mallory said, "are not on the Crown's payroll." He snapped the watch shut and turned away, which was as close as he came to forgiving anyone. "The *Gannet* is in from Ostrey. Forty barrels salt cod, twelve bales wool, and a captain who swears blind he has no brandy aboard. Go and find his brandy."

She found it in under an hour, in a false bulkhead behind the cable tier that a child could have tapped out, and she wrote it into the tide-book in her small upright hand while the captain of the *Gannet* stood at her elbow explaining that he had never seen those casks in his life. Then she went back up to the long room under the eaves where the clerks sat, and took off her wet boots, and put her feet on the brazier rail, and opened the ledgers for the month.

It was the kind of work she was good at and nobody else wanted. Every ship that came into Saltgate came into the tide-book: her name, her master, her lading, the hour she crossed the bar. Every ship that did not come in, that went down on the Tithe Rocks or the long shoals off Carrow Head, went into the loss-book instead, with a line drawn under her name in red ink and a note of what the Crown was owed for her. The two books were kept by different hands and audited by a third, and Tamsin had always found something restful in that. Three people had to agree before a ship could be said to exist.

She was copying the loss-book's figures into the quarter-day abstract when she came to the *Heron*.

*Heron*, brig, master Jory Callender, out of Pellmouth with wine and dyed cloth. Struck on the Tithe Rocks in the gale of the fourth. All hands lost. Cargo lost. Assessed for the Crown's portion at three hundred and forty marks. Under it, the red line, and the harbourmaster's initials: *O.H.*

Tamsin put her pen down.

She had seen the *Heron* on the sixth. She was almost sure of it. She had been on the Mole with Pell, the boy who ran messages for the clerks, buying hot mussels from the woman with the cart, and there had been a brig warping into the inner basin with a heron carved under her bowsprit — not a good heron, a lumpy thing with its neck too short — and Pell had laughed at it and said it looked like his aunt.

Two days after she had gone down with all hands.

"You've stopped," said Mallory, behind her. He moved quietly for a big man. He was the only person in the Customs House who could come up the stairs without the third tread groaning.

"The *Heron*," she said. "Struck on the Tithes on the fourth."

"Yes. Bad business. Callender was a decent sort, for a Pellmouth man." He leaned over her shoulder. He smelled of wet wool and the clove pastilles he sucked for his chest. "What of it?"

"I think I saw her. On the sixth. In the inner basin."

Mallory said nothing for long enough that she turned round to look at him. His eyes were on the line of red ink.

"You think," he said.

"There was a heron on the bow. A bad one. Pell said it looked like his aunt."

"Pell says everything looks like his aunt. Pell's aunt is the most widely resembled woman in Saltgate." But he did not laugh, and he did not move away. "There are other brigs with birds on them, Tamsin."

"I know."

"The *Curlew*. The *Kittiwake*. Half the coasting trade is named for something with feathers."

"I know," she said again. "It's only that the *Heron*'s not in the tide-book for the sixth. Nothing's in the tide-book for the sixth. No brig at all came over the bar that day. I've just been through it."

"Then you were mistaken about the day."

"Then I was mistaken about the day," she agreed, and picked up her pen.

He stood there a moment longer. Outside the window the tide had turned and the boats in the basin were swinging slowly round on their moorings to face the sea, all together, like a congregation rising. A gull walked along the gutter and looked in at them with one cold yellow eye.

"Copy it as it stands," Mallory said at last. "Initial it. Then go home, you've been at that abstract since the bell and you look like something the Mole washed up." He put his hand on her shoulder, briefly, heavily, and took it away. "And Tamsin. Don't mention the *Heron* to your uncle."

"Why not?"

"Because he signed it," Mallory said, "and he's had a bad month, and I'd like him to have a better one." He went back down the long room and down the stair to his own office, and the third tread did not groan, and she sat looking at the red line and the two neat letters under it until the ink on her own pen had dried to a crust.

She copied it as it stood. She initialled it. Then, because she was the kind of person who could not leave a thing alone once it had a corner turned up, she tore a scrap off the corner of the abstract and wrote on it *Heron — 6th — inner basin — ask Pell*, and folded it small, and put it in her boot.

scenes.title: The Gull and Lantern
scenes.text:
The Gull and Lantern stood where the Mole met the old town wall, so that half its windows looked at the sea and half at the backs of the tanneries, and Nessa Brack charged accordingly. Tamsin took a seat on the tannery side because it was cheaper and because nobody she knew would be sitting there.

She was wrong about that.

"Clerk Vey," said a voice, and someone dropped into the chair across from her without asking, and set down two cups of something hot that smelled of pepper and burnt sugar. "You look like you need this more than I do. Which is saying a great deal, because I need it a very great deal."

"Captain Ashcombe."

"Bel, please. Captain makes me feel like I ought to be wearing a hat." Bel Ashcombe was perhaps thirty, brown as tanned sailcloth from the weather, with grey eyes and a gold ring through one ear and a manner of sitting in a chair as though the chair had been built specifically for the purpose and was grateful. She had been fined by the Customs House eleven times in the four years Tamsin had worked there, and had paid every fine promptly, in good coin, with a smile, which Mallory said was the most suspicious thing about her. "I hear you found Haddon's brandy."

"How do you hear these things?"

"I drink in the Gull. Everyone hears everything in the Gull. Nessa puts it in the beer." Bel pushed one of the cups across. "Go on. It isn't poisoned. If I wanted to poison a tide-clerk I'd do it somewhere with better light, so I could watch."

Tamsin drank. It was very good, and very strong, and she felt it go down into the cold place behind her breastbone that had been there since the morning.

"Haddon's a fool," Bel went on. "Behind the cable tier. I ask you. My grandmother could have found it and she's been dead since the old king."

"Where would you have put it?"

Bel smiled. "Somewhere you'd never look, Clerk Vey. That's rather the point of me."

Across the room Nessa Brack was arguing with a drover about the price of a pie. She was a broad, red-armed woman with a voice that had been built for calling across water, and she did not lower it for anybody. Behind her, over the bar, hung the lantern the house was named for: an old ship's lantern, green copper gone to verdigris, with a gull painted on its glass so long ago that only the shape of the wings was left.

"Do you know a brig called the *Heron*?" Tamsin said.

She had not meant to say it. It was the drink, or the warmth, or the way Bel was looking at her, as if she were a puzzle that had turned out to be more interesting than the box suggested.

Bel's face did not change at all, which was itself a sort of change. "Callender's boat. Went down on the Tithes."

"So I'm told."

"You're told right. Terrible night, the fourth. I was out in it myself. I'd have gone down too if the *Merrow* weren't the best-found lugger on this coast." She turned her cup round on the table, once, a full circle. "Why?"

"No reason."

"Clerks don't ask about wrecks for no reason. Clerks ask about wrecks because there's money in them for the Crown." Bel leaned back. "Or for somebody."

Tamsin said nothing. The fire popped. Somebody on the sea side of the room began to sing, badly, a song about a girl in Ostrey with a wooden leg.

"Here's some free advice," Bel said, more quietly. "Which is the only kind I give, as you'll have noticed from my fines. The Tithe Rocks take a lot of ships. More than they used to. The insurers in Pellmouth have started grumbling about it, and the magistrate has started telling them it's the weather. And when the magistrate of Saltgate says it's the weather, the sensible people of Saltgate look up at the sky and agree with him." She finished her drink. "You strike me as sensible, Clerk Vey. Mostly."

"Mostly?"

"You came into the Gull alone after dark and sat with your back to the door." Bel stood, and dropped a coin on the table for both cups, and put on a coat that had once belonged to a much larger and more respectable person. "Goodnight. Mind the Stair. It's slick when the fog's in."

She was gone before Tamsin could think of an answer. Tamsin sat looking at the door, and then at the lantern, and then at the coin, which was a Pellmouth half-mark, new-minted, the king's face still sharp on it.

She was still sitting there twenty minutes later when Pell came in out of the fog, small and wet and important, and came between the tables to her as straight as a dropped stone.

"Message," he said. "From Master Mallory. He says come to the Customs House at first light. Not the long room. His office. He says don't tell nobody."

"Anybody."

"He said nobody." Pell wiped his nose on his sleeve. "He gave me a whole penny for it, so it must be important. Is it about the bird-boat?"

Tamsin looked at him. "What bird-boat?"

"The one with my aunt on the front." He grinned, gap-toothed. "Master Mallory asked me about it. This afternoon, after you went home. He asked me what day it was, and I said it was the day the mussel woman had the fight with the fish woman, and he went all quiet and gave me the penny." He considered. "That might have been for that, actually. Not the message. I might get another penny for the message."

"You might," Tamsin said, and gave him one, and sat a while longer after he had gone, with her hand flat on the table over the Pellmouth coin, listening to the man on the sea side of the room get to the verse about the wooden leg.

scenes.title: The letter
scenes.text:
Mallory's office was a narrow room at the seaward end of the Customs House, and at first light it was the coldest room in Saltgate. He had not lit the stove. He was sitting behind his desk in his coat, with his hat still on, and when Tamsin came in he looked up at her as though he had forgotten he had sent for her and was trying to remember why.

"Shut the door," he said. "Lock it."

She did. The key was stiff, and she had to lean on it.

"Sit."

She sat. On the desk between them, squared exactly to its edge the way he squared everything, lay a letter. It was folded in three and had been sealed, and the seal had been broken cleanly with a knife rather than torn, so that the wax still held its shape: a tower, and a key across the tower, and round the rim a line of lettering too small to read from where she sat.

"You were right about the *Heron*," Mallory said.

Tamsin found she felt nothing about that. She had expected to feel vindicated, or frightened, and instead there was only a sort of flatness, the feeling of a step that is not there in the dark.

"Pell told me," she said.

"Pell tells everyone everything. It's why I pay him." He touched the letter with one finger, not quite pushing it toward her. "I went down to the harbourmaster's office last night, after the bell. Your uncle had gone home. I have a key, as assessor; I'm entitled to inspect his books at any hour, though I can't remember the last time anybody did. I wanted to see his pilot's log for the sixth. Every ship that crosses the bar takes a pilot, and every pilot is entered."

"And the *Heron* was entered."

"The *Heron* was not entered. The page for the sixth has been cut out. Very neatly. With a knife, up against the binding, so you'd have to count the leaves to know." He breathed out through his nose. "So I counted the leaves, and then I looked in the places a man keeps things he shouldn't, and I found this at the back of his desk, behind the drawer, where you'd have to take the drawer right out."

"You took my uncle's desk apart."

"I did." He met her eyes. He had very pale eyes, Mallory, almost colourless, and in the grey light from the window they were like water in a basin. "Read it."

She unfolded the letter. The hand was a good one, a lawyer's hand, all its letters joined. It was not long.

*O. — The H. is in the Quarter, berth under the old chandlery. Cargo to be off by the ninth and the vessel broken by the twelfth. The loss is entered and the Pellmouth underwriters have paid on it. Your portion as before. Burn this. — T.*

Under it, as though the writer had paused and come back to it, a further line in the same hand but smaller, cramped in against the bottom edge: *The ledger stays with you. If it leaves your keeping it leaves mine.*

Tamsin read it twice. Then she put it down on the desk, squared to the edge, the way he had had it.

"T," she said.

"Tower and key," Mallory said. "It's the seal of the magistrate's court. Anybody in the court could have used it. Any clerk, any bailiff." He did not sound as though he believed this. "But it's Corvan Thale's court, and it's Corvan Thale's hand, and I've seen it on enough warrants to know it in the dark."

"What ledger?"

"I don't know." For the first time he looked tired, really tired, an old man in a cold room with his hat on. "I've been sitting here since four trying to think what ledger. The tide-book's ours. The loss-book's ours. The harbourmaster's log is your uncle's, but that's not a ledger, that's a log, and Thale would know the difference — he's a pedant, it's the only thing I like about him." He rubbed his eyes. "There's a second set of books somewhere. There must be. You can't do this more than once without keeping count of who's been paid, and they've done it more than once. I went back through the loss-book last night. Nineteen wrecks on the Tithes in three years. In the three years before that, four."

"Nineteen," Tamsin said.

"I want you to keep this." He pushed the letter across to her, properly this time. "Not here. Not at your uncle's house. Somewhere else. Somewhere nobody would think of."

"Why me?"

"Because if anything happens to me," Mallory said, quite calmly, "they'll come here first, and then they'll go to my rooms, and they'll find nothing in either place, and they will think that's the end of it. Nobody looks at a tide-clerk. That's your great advantage, Tamsin. You are a person nobody looks at." He almost smiled. "I mean that as a compliment. I've spent my whole life trying to be one."

"Nothing is going to happen to you."

"No, I don't expect so." He stood, and took his hat off at last, and turned it round in his hands. "I'm going to Pellmouth tomorrow, to see a man I know. One of the insurers. If I can get the Pellmouth men to ask the right questions in the right court, it stops being Saltgate's business and becomes the Crown's, and Thale can explain his weather to the King's Bench." He put the hat back on. "Go to work. Act like a person with nothing in her boot."

She looked down at her boot without meaning to. He did smile then, a little.

"Pell," he said. "Again. Go on."

She went. At the door she turned to say something — she never afterwards knew what — and he had sat back down behind his desk in the cold and had turned to the window, where the light was coming up the colour of pewter and a fog was lying on the basin so thick the masts stood up out of it like reeds.

scenes.title: Under the Lantern Stair
scenes.text:
They found him at the turn of the afternoon tide, when the water went out from under the Lantern Stair and left the bottom steps bare and green and running.

It was a boy who found him, one of the mussel-pickers, and he screamed, and by the time Tamsin got there from the Customs House half the Mole was standing at the top of the Stair looking down.

The Stair went from the old town straight down the face of the sea-wall to the water, a hundred and twelve steps cut into the rock, with an iron lantern on a bracket every twenty; at high water you could step off the last of them into a boat. At low water there were nine more steps below that, slimed and treacherous, that nobody used, and Mallory was lying across the lowest of them on his back, with one arm flung out and his face turned up to the sky and full of water.

His hat was gone. That was the thing she kept looking at. She had never seen him without his hat out of doors, and his head seemed very small without it, and the thin grey hair was flat to his skull.

"Back," somebody was saying. "Back, all of you, give them room —"

The magistrate's men were coming down the Stair in their blue coats, and behind them, picking his way with a hand on the rail, was the magistrate himself.

Corvan Thale was not a tall man, but he held himself as if he were, and people moved aside for him on the steps without being asked. He was perhaps fifty, clean-shaven, with a long clever face and dark hair going silver at the temples, very neatly cut. He wore a black coat and a white stock and no ornament but the court's ring on his left hand, and he looked down at Mallory's body the way Tamsin had seen him look at a badly drawn deed, with a sort of patient regret.

Behind him came her uncle.

Orrin Hask was harbourmaster of Saltgate and had been for twenty years, and Tamsin had lived in his house since she was nine, and she had never seen him as he was now. He was a big man run to softness, with a red weathered face and a beard he kept short because his late wife had liked it short, and the red had gone out of his face entirely. He looked as though someone had pulled a plug in him and drained it.

"Idris," he said. "Oh, Idris, you old fool."

"You knew him well, harbourmaster?" Thale said.

"Thirty years." Orrin's voice cracked. "Thirty years, near enough."

"Then perhaps you can tell me whether he was a drinking man."

There was a small silence on the Stair.

"No," said Orrin. "No more than any of us."

"He'd been drinking today," said one of the blue coats, a sergeant, crouched by the body. He held up a flask. "This was in his coat. It's near empty."

"Mallory didn't drink," said Tamsin, before she could stop herself.

Thale turned and looked up the steps at her. She had a moment's impression of being weighed, accurately and without malice, the way she herself weighed a bale of wool for duty.

"And you are?"

"She's my niece," said Orrin quickly. "Tamsin. She clerks for the Customs House. She worked for him."

"Ah." Thale inclined his head to her, very slightly. "Then I'm sorry for your loss, Clerk Vey. It's a hard thing, to lose a master you respected." He said it as though he meant it. Perhaps he did. "But men are often not, in private, what they are at their desks. The steps are slick at low water, and it's been foggy all morning, and he was not a young man." He turned back to the sergeant. "Note it as misadventure. Have him carried up to the dead-house and send for his family. Has he family?"

"A sister," said Orrin. "In Carrow."

"Send to Carrow." Thale glanced up at the sky. The fog had burnt off at noon, and now the sun was out, weak and white, glittering off the wet steps. "Well. It's a fine afternoon for it, at least."

He went back up the Stair. Her uncle stood a moment longer looking down at Mallory, and then he followed, and he did not look at Tamsin as he passed her, and she understood that he was not looking at her very carefully.

She stayed. The blue coats rolled Mallory into a sailcloth and carried him up, grunting, and the crowd went with them, and after a while there was nobody on the bottom of the Stair but Tamsin and the gulls. The tide was beginning to come back in. It came in fast under the Stair; it always had.

There was something white in the weed on the second-lowest step.

She went down for it, holding the rail, her boots sliding. It was a clove pastille, half-dissolved, the kind he had always had in his waistcoat pocket. Beside it, jammed into a crack in the rock where the water would have been at high tide, was the brim of a hat. She worked it free. It had been torn half off its crown, the felt ripped, as though someone had held it — or held the head in it — and twisted.

She stood with the hat in her hands while the water came up over her boots, over the letter folded small in its scrap of oilcloth inside the left one, and did not move until it was at her shins and so cold she could not feel her feet.

scenes.title: Supper
scenes.text:
Her uncle had not lit the fire either. It seemed to be a day for that.

He was sitting at the kitchen table when she came in, in his shirtsleeves, the old brass tide-key on its cord at his open collar, with a bottle in front of him that had not been opened, and he glanced up when the door went and something in his face shut, very fast, like a shutter coming down on a shop.

"You're soaked," he said.

"I went down to the bottom of the Stair."

"What for?"

She put the hat on the table between them. For a long moment he did not touch it.

"That's his," he said.

"It was in a crack in the rock. One step up from where he was lying. It's been torn." She heard her own voice and it sounded level, like a clerk reading out a lading. "He didn't fall, Uncle. Somebody held him under."

"You don't know that."

"I know he didn't drink. I know he was going to Pellmouth tomorrow. He told me so this morning."

That landed. She saw it land. Orrin put both hands flat on the table, either side of the bottle, as though the table had moved.

"This morning," he said. "You saw him this morning."

"He sent for me."

"What did he want?"

And there it was: the place where she could have told him. She looked at him across the table, at the big soft hands, at the beard Aunt Marra had liked short, at the man who had taught her to read the tide-tables when she was ten and walked her to the Customs House on her first day, and put his arms round her on the step, and stood outside it for an hour, she found out later, in case she came out crying. *Don't mention the Heron to your uncle. Because he signed it.*

"He wanted me in early," she said. "There was a brandy matter. On the *Gannet*."

Her uncle closed his eyes.

"Tamsin," he said, without opening them. "I want you to listen to me. Whatever Idris thought he had — whatever he told you — he was an old man and he saw plots in the drains. He always did. The magistrate says it was the fog and the steps, and the magistrate is right. Do you understand me?" He opened his eyes, and they were wet. "The magistrate is right."

"It wasn't foggy," she said. "Not by the afternoon. The sun was out."

"Go to bed."

"Uncle —"

"Go to bed, Tamsin. Please." He picked up the bottle, and looked at it, and put it down again unopened. "Please. For me."

She went up. She did not undress. She sat on the end of her bed in the dark with her wet boots still on, and after a long time she heard him go out — the front door, and his heavy tread down the lane toward the harbour, at an hour when there was no reason for the harbourmaster of Saltgate to be going anywhere at all.

scenes.title: The road to Hollin
scenes.text:
Hollin Abbey stood four miles up the coast on a headland of thin grass and thrift, and there was no road to it, only a cart track that the sea had been eating a yard at a time for as long as anyone could remember. Tamsin walked it in the morning with the letter in her boot and Mallory's hat wrapped in a cloth under her arm, because she had not been able to think what else to do with either of them.

She had told the Customs House she was ill. Nobody had argued. The long room had been very quiet when she put her head round the door, and one of the older clerks, Fennick, who had never said more than ten words to her together, had got up from his desk and come over and said, *Go home, girl. Go home and stay there,* and squeezed her arm so hard it hurt.

The wind was off the sea and smelled of rain, though none had fallen yet. Below her, on the left, the water was the colour of slate, and far out on it a single sail was beating up the coast against the wind — a lugger, she thought, from the cut of it. Gulls hung in the updraught at the cliff edge without moving their wings.

Sister Wren was in the scriptorium, where she always was, and she did not seem surprised to see her.

"You've grown," she said, which was what she always said, although Tamsin had not grown since she was fifteen and was now twenty-four. Sister Wren Oduya was small and very upright and very old, with a face like a walnut and eyes that had gone milky at the edges and were still sharper than anyone's in the middle. She had taught Tamsin her letters, and her numbers, and the long patient art of finding the one wrong figure in a column of four hundred, in the years when Orrin had paid the abbey to take his dead sister's child off his hands for six hours a day. "Sit down. You look terrible. Is it the Mallory business?"

"How do you know about that?"

"The fish woman comes up on Thursdays." Wren set down her pen. "She says he fell on the Stair drunk. She says it with a great deal of relish. I don't believe a word of it; Idris Mallory took the pledge in this very room thirty years ago, and I was the one who wrote it out for him." She folded her hands. "So. What have you brought me?"

Tamsin took off her boot.

Wren read the letter by the window, holding it so close to her face that her nose almost touched the paper. She read it a long time. Then she turned it over and looked at the back, and held it up to the light, and turned it again.

"This is a copy," she said.

"What?"

"Not the words. The words are as they were first written. But it's been written twice. Look." She held it out, angled to the window, and pointed with one dry fingertip. "Here, and here — you see? Under the ink. A dry point. Somebody laid this sheet over another and went over the lines with a stylus first, to get the spacing, and then inked it. A clerk's trick. I taught it to you myself."

Tamsin looked. Once she knew to look, she could see it: a faint, colourless groove under each stroke, like the ghost of a second hand.

"Why would anyone copy a letter," she said slowly, "and seal the copy?"

"So that the original could be kept," said Wren. "Somebody wanted the harbourmaster to have this. And somebody wanted to keep the real one somewhere safe. Which means somebody, at least, does not altogether trust Master Hask." She put the letter down. "Do you know what the ledger is?"

"No. Mallory thought it was a second set of books. A record of who'd been paid."

"Mallory was very likely right. He usually was, about money; it was people he couldn't read." Wren was silent a moment. "You know, I think, that the abbey holds the Crown's copy of the harbour charter."

"I didn't."

"Nobody does. It's very dull. But under the charter the harbourmaster is obliged to keep a salt-book — a book of the salt tithe owed on every cargo landed. It hasn't been collected since the old king remitted it, forty years ago. But the obligation was never struck out of the charter, so the harbourmaster still has to keep the book. A dead book, for a dead tax. Every harbourmaster since has kept one, and filled it in, and nobody has ever once opened it." She looked at Tamsin with her sharp milky eyes. "If I wanted to keep a second set of accounts in plain sight, in a harbour office, I can't think of a better place than a book that the law requires to exist and nobody has read in forty years."

"The salt ledger," Tamsin said.

"I imagine that's what they'd call it, yes. The men who use it." Wren reached across and put her old hand over Tamsin's. It was very cold and very light, like a bird's foot. "Tamsin. Listen to me. If that book is what we think, then your uncle has been keeping it. You know that."

"Yes."

"Do you know what you're going to do?"

"No," said Tamsin. And then, because it was Wren and you did not lie to Wren, you could not, she had never once got away with it: "I'm going to find it."

scenes.title: A visitor from the sea
scenes.text:
It began to rain at noon, hard, coming in sideways off the headland and rattling on the scriptorium's leaded panes, and Sister Wren made her stay and eat soup in the warming room with the four other sisters who were left, all of them nearly as old as Wren and none of them nearly as alert.

Wren did not eat. She sat at the end of the table with the letter flat beside her bowl and a sheet of the abbey's good paper, and copied it, letter for letter, seal and all, in her tiny upright hand, and when she had finished she sanded it and folded it and gave the original back to Tamsin without a word, and put the copy in her sleeve.

Tamsin had not known she was hungry. She ate two bowls.

She was halfway through the second when the porter's bell rang at the gate, and kept ringing, and Sister Agathe went out grumbling with her shawl over her head and came back a few minutes later looking scandalised.

"There's a *woman*," she said, as if this were a new and unwelcome category of thing, "at the gate. From a *boat*. Asking for the clerk."

It was Bel Ashcombe, of course. She was standing in the gatehouse arch with the rain sheeting off the stone behind her, in her enormous coat, wet to the skin, with her hair plastered flat to her head and her gold earring dripping.

"Clerk Vey," she said. "You walk very fast for a woman with a broken heart."

"How did you know I was here?"

"I saw you on the cliff path this morning. I was standing off the point." Bel jerked her head at the sea, where the lugger Tamsin had seen was lying at anchor in the lee of the headland, pitching on the swell, her sails brailed up. "I've been sitting out there all morning, and the last of it in the rain, trying to decide whether to come in, and in the end I decided I'd get less wet in here than out there, which I'm sorry to say was a miscalculation." She glanced past Tamsin into the cloister, at Sister Agathe hovering with her shawl. "Is there somewhere we can talk? Somewhere without nuns?"

There was not, really. In the end they sat in the porter's lodge, with the door shut and the brazier lit and Sister Agathe almost certainly listening on the other side of it. Bel took her coat off and hung it over the brazier to steam, and sat down on the porter's stool with her elbows on her knees.

"I liked Idris Mallory," she said. "I want you to know that first. He fined me eleven times and every time he was right, and he never once pretended he wasn't enjoying it. That's a kind of honesty you don't often get." She looked at her hands. "I'm sorry. That's all. I wanted to say it to somebody who'd know what I meant."

"Thank you," said Tamsin. She found she meant it.

"That's not why I came, though." Bel looked up. "You asked me about the *Heron*."

"Yes."

"I told you she went down on the Tithes."

"Yes."

"She didn't." Bel took a breath, the way you would before going into cold water. "A week ago a man came to me in the Gull. Not a man I knew. He wanted a boat to go into the Drowned Quarter at night, at the top of the tide, and take off some cargo from a brig lying there, and run it up the coast to Carrow, no questions. He paid half in advance. Pellmouth coin, new-minted." She reached into her shirt and pulled out a half-mark on a thong — the twin of the one she had left on the table at the Gull. "I kept one. I don't know why. Superstition."

"And you did it."

"I did it." Bel's mouth twisted. "I'm a smuggler, Clerk Vey. That's what smuggling is. Somebody gives you money to carry things in the dark and you don't ask what they are. And I'd have gone on not asking, except that when I came alongside her in the Quarter, the brig I was taking cargo off had a heron under her bowsprit. A bad one. Neck too short."

"Pell's aunt," said Tamsin.

Bel stared at her. "What?"

"Nothing. Go on."

"There's not much more. We took off forty casks of Pellmouth red and a lot of dyed cloth, and ran it up to Carrow, and a cart met us on the beach, and that was that. Afterwards I heard in the Gull she'd been entered lost on the fourth, with all hands. And I thought, well, that's strange, but there's a lot of strange in this trade and most of it's none of mine." She turned the coin over in her fingers. "And then Idris Mallory was found under the Lantern Stair, and somebody told me he'd been asking questions about the *Heron* all over the Mole the day before. And I thought: they'll come to me next. Whoever *they* are. Because I'm the only one outside of it who saw her afloat."

"Except Pell," said Tamsin. "And me."

They looked at each other across the brazier. The rain hammered on the lodge roof.

"Who was the man?" Tamsin said. "The one in the Gull."

"I don't know his name. Tall. Thin. Bad teeth. He wore a blue coat, but not a court coat — no facings. Like a man who used to wear one." Bel shrugged. "I'd know him again."

"The magistrate's men wear blue."

"So do a lot of people." But Bel's eyes had gone very still. "You think it's Thale."

Tamsin took off her boot again.

Bel read the letter the way she seemed to do everything, fast, all at once, and then she sat back on the stool and let out a long low whistle that Sister Agathe on the other side of the door must have heard.

"Oh, Clerk Vey," she said softly. "Oh, you poor fool. You've got the magistrate of Saltgate in your boot."

"I know."

"And your uncle."

"I know."

"What are you going to do?"

It was the second time that day she had been asked, and she gave the same answer, and found that it was easier the second time.

"Go into the Quarter," she said. "Find the *Heron*. Find whatever's left of her. And then find the book." She looked at Bel. "I could use a boat."

Bel considered her for a long moment, and then, slowly, began to grin.

"I was afraid you'd say that," she said.

scenes.title: Slack water
scenes.text:
The Drowned Quarter had been the richest part of Saltgate once, before the great storm in the old king's time took the outer sea-wall and let the water in. Now it was a district of streets that were canals at high tide and mud at low, of warehouses standing up to their first-floor windows in the sea, of chandleries and counting-houses with weed growing out of their door-knockers. People still lived there, a few, in the upper storeys, and went about by punt. Nobody who could live anywhere else did.

They went in at slack water on the top of the tide, two nights after the abbey, in the *Merrow*'s little dinghy with the oars muffled in sacking. Bel rowed. Tamsin sat in the stern with a shuttered lantern between her knees and Mallory's hat — she had not been able to leave it — rolled up and stuffed inside her coat, where it made a lump against her ribs like a second heart.

"Under the old chandlery," Bel said, low. "There were three chandleries in the Quarter. Abel Stott's, which fell in. Gammon's, which is a brothel now. And the Guild chandlery, on the Ropewalk, which is the one with the big doors at water level. That's the one I went into. You could float a brig in through those doors at the top of a spring tide, if you knew what you were doing and didn't mind the paint."

"And if they broke her up by the twelfth, like the letter says?"

"Then we'll find a lot of firewood and I'll have rowed you about in the dark for nothing, and you'll owe me a drink." Bel feathered an oar, and the dinghy slid round a corner between two black walls so close Tamsin could have touched both. "It's the fourteenth. If she's still there, they're behind."

The water was very still. It smelled of rot and salt and, faintly, of tar. Somewhere above them a window was lit, a single yellow square high up in a wall, and as they passed under it Tamsin heard a woman singing to a baby, the same three notes over and over, and then the corner took them and the singing was gone.

The moon came out from behind the cloud. It was nearly full, and it laid a long white road down the canal ahead of them, and at the end of the road, where the canal widened into what had been a square, the Guild chandlery stood up out of the water with its great doors open like a mouth.

Bel stopped rowing.

"Those were shut," she said. "A week ago. They were shut and barred, and a man had to come down and open them for us."

"Maybe they've finished with her."

"Maybe." Bel did not sound as if she believed it. She sat with the oars dripping, looking at the doors. "Or maybe somebody wants us to think they've finished."

"Us?"

"Anybody." Bel shook herself. "Never mind. I've been in this trade too long, I see revenue men in my soup. Get the lantern ready. Don't open it till I say."

She brought them in under the lintel, slowly, the dinghy's bow nosing into the dark like a dog into a strange house. Inside the air was colder and the smell of tar was much stronger. Tamsin could hear water moving, slapping softly against something big, and the creak of timber under strain.

"Now," said Bel.

Tamsin opened the shutter.

The *Heron* lay in the middle of the flooded warehouse floor with her masts out and her bowsprit gone, half-stripped, her planking torn away down one side so that the ribs showed white in the lantern-light like the bones of something that had been eaten. There were tools on her deck, mauls and crowbars and a big two-man saw with its blade still in a cut, as if the men using it had simply put it down and walked away in the middle of a stroke. They had started breaking her up, and then stopped.

The figurehead was lying on the deck by the foremast stump, where somebody had pried it off and dropped it. A heron. A bad one. Its neck too short.

"Well," said Bel softly. "Hello, Pell's aunt."

scenes.title: The boy on the gallery
scenes.text:
There was a gallery round three sides of the warehouse at what would have been first-floor height, a loading gallery with cranes on it and a long row of bays where the Guild had once kept its cordage, and it was from the gallery that the voice came.

"Miss Tamsin?"

She nearly dropped the lantern. Bel swore, a short ugly sea-word, and her hand went inside her coat for something.

"Miss Tamsin, it's me. Don't shine it, you'll blind me."

"Pell?"

He came out to the edge of the gallery and peered down at them, small and pale, holding on to a crane post. He was soaked to the waist and had weed in his hair, and he looked delighted with himself.

"I followed you," he said. "From the Mole. I saw you go down to the lugger and I thought, she's going after the bird-boat, and I came along the roofs. You can get nearly all the way along the roofs if you're not big. There's only one jump and it's not even very far." He considered. "It was quite far. And then there's the wading bit, by the old wall, but it's only up to here."

"Pell, you idiot," said Tamsin, "you absolute — come down. Come down *now*, we're going —"

"There's things up here," Pell said. "In the bays. Boxes. Lots of them. With writing on." He was already turning away. "Come and see. There's a ladder at the end, it's mostly all right."

Bel looked at Tamsin. Tamsin looked at Bel.

"Two minutes," said Bel. "Then we're gone, boy or no boy."

The ladder was mostly all right. Tamsin went up it with the lantern hooked over her wrist and Bel below her, and at the top Pell was waiting by the first of the cordage bays with his eyes enormous.

The boxes were stacked to the ceiling. Not boxes: crates, cases, casks, bales wrapped in oilcloth and stencilled with merchants' marks. Tamsin moved along the bays with the lantern held high and read them the way she would have read a lading at the Customs House, without meaning to. *Callender, Pellmouth.* *Rook & Daughter, Ostrey.* *Saint-Aubin, by the Narrows.* *Gilly, Carrow.* Wine and cloth and copper and spice and a hundred and one other things, a whole harbour's worth of trade, in the dark.

"These are wrecks," she said. Her voice sounded strange to her. "Bel. These are all wrecks. I know these names. The *Rook*'s *Fortunate*. Gilly's *Swallow*. They're in the loss-book. They're all in the loss-book. Every one."

"How many?"

She did the arithmetic without wanting to; she could not help it. "Nineteen," she said. "I think there's something from every one of the nineteen."

"Then they aren't taking it to Carrow any more," said Bel. "They're keeping it. Waiting for a buyer, or —" She stopped. "Shut the lantern."

"What?"

"*Shut it.*"

Tamsin shut it. The dark came down. And in the dark, below them and away toward the great doors, she heard what Bel had heard: the knock of oars in rowlocks, unmuffled, and men's voices, and the scrape of a boat's keel coming in over the sill.

scenes.title: What she carried out
scenes.text:
There were four of them, in a big flat-bottomed punt, and they had lanterns of their own and did not trouble to shutter them. Tamsin lay flat on the gallery floor between two stacks of crates with her cheek against the boards and watched them through a gap, and Bel lay beside her, and Pell lay on her other side, breathing very fast through his nose.

"Somebody's been in," one of the men said. He was holding his lantern up toward the *Heron*. "There's a boat. Look — there, by the stern."

"That's the *Merrow*'s tender," said another voice. "That's Ashcombe's."

Tamsin felt Bel go rigid.

"She's here, then. Search the gallery." The first man turned, and the lantern swung up, and Tamsin saw his face: long, thin, with bad teeth, under a blue coat with no facings. "And somebody go and tell him she's here. He'll want to know."

"Tell who?" said Pell.

He said it in a whisper. He said it as softly as Tamsin had ever heard him say anything. But the warehouse was all water and bare stone, and it carried the way sound carries in a church, and every lantern in the punt turned toward the gallery at once.

What happened next Tamsin was never afterwards able to put in order. She remembered Bel shoving her, hard, toward the end of the gallery away from the ladder, and shouting *roofs*, and she remembered Pell's hand in hers and then not in hers. She remembered a crate going over the edge into the water with a noise like a cannon. She remembered running along a bay in the pitch dark with her arms out in front of her and hitting a wall, and a window in it, and the window giving, all at once, with a crack of rotten frame — and the cold air, and a slope of slates under her hands and knees, and the moon.

She remembered, too, that as she went along the bay she had put out a hand and caught at something to steady herself, and it had come away from the top of a stack: a book, leather-bound, flat, with a cord round it. She had not decided to take it. Her fingers had simply closed on it the way they closed on a pen.

She got along the roofs. She did not know how. There was only one jump, and Pell had been right that it was quite far. On the far side of it she lay on her back on a parapet with the book clutched to her chest and the hat still somehow inside her coat and listened to the shouting behind her in the Quarter, a long way off, and then not so far off, and then dying away.

Then she sat up and looked back for the others.

There was nobody on the roofs behind her. Nobody at all. Down in the canal below, at the corner by the chandlery, a lantern moved on the water: the punt, going away slowly toward the Ropewalk. There were five figures in it now, not four. One of them was much smaller than the others, and was not sitting up by itself.

Of Bel and the *Merrow*'s dinghy there was no sign.

Tamsin sat on the parapet for a long time. The moon went behind the cloud and came out again. At last she untied the cord round the book with fingers that did not feel like hers and opened it, and held it up to the moonlight, and read on its first page, in a fine joined lawyer's hand she now knew very well — the heading only; the entries under it were in a clerk's cramped hand — a list of names and figures under a heading that said only *Salt, by the Quarter Day*.

It was not the ledger. She knew that almost at once. It was a ledger — a tally of the cargo in the bays, ship by ship, with sums against it — but it was a warehouseman's book, a working copy, and on the inside of its back board somebody had written, in a different and much worse hand, *Fair copy to O.H. as before*.

O.H. Not T. The book she wanted was still in her uncle's keeping.

And Thale's men had Pell.

scenes.title: The harbour office
scenes.text:
The harbourmaster's office stood at the root of the Mole, a squat stone building with a lamp-room on top where the harbour light had burned before they built the new one out on the point. Orrin kept it as he kept everything, which was to say not well: there were charts on every wall, curling at the corners, and tide-tables nailed over the charts, and pilots' chits spiked on nails over the tide-tables, and a smell of lamp-oil and wet dog although he had not had a dog in eleven years.

He was there when she came in at dawn. She had known he would be. He was sitting at his desk with the drawer out — the whole drawer, out of its runners and on the floor by his feet — and he was staring into the empty space at the back where it had been, where Mallory had put his hand.

"It's gone," he said without turning round. "The letter. I knew it was gone. I've known since Idris. I just kept looking."

"I have it," Tamsin said.

He turned round then. She did not know what she looked like — she had not been home; she had sat on the parapet till the tide went down and then come along the shore under the sea-wall, wading where she had to — but from his face it was bad.

"Where's the boy?" he said.

So he knew that too. Thale's men had been to him in the night, then — or he had gone to them, the way he had gone the night Mallory died.

"Thale has him," she said. "Thale's men. They came into the Guild chandlery last night while we were there. Bel Ashcombe was with me. I don't know where she is. I think she got away. I don't know." She put the warehouseman's book on his desk, on top of the tide-tables. "I took this."

He did not look at the book. He went on looking at her.

"Why didn't you come to me?" he said. "After Idris. Why didn't you come to me?"

"Because you signed the *Heron*," she said. "Mallory told me. He said not to tell you. He said you'd had a bad month." She heard her voice crack and did not care. "Was it a bad month, Uncle? Was it a bad three years? Nineteen ships. Nineteen ships and their crews' families paid off with a line of red ink and the Crown's portion in Thale's pocket and some of it in yours, and Mallory under the Stair with his face full of water. Was that a bad month?"

Orrin put his face in his hands.

She had thought she wanted to see that. She found she did not. She stood in the cold office in her wet clothes and watched her uncle cry, the big shoulders shaking, and felt nothing but tired, so tired she could have lain down on the flagstones and slept.

"I didn't know about Idris," he said through his fingers. "I swear to you, Tamsin. On Marra's grave. I didn't know they'd do that. He said he'd talk to him. Thale said he'd *talk* to him."

"And you believed him."

"I wanted to." He lowered his hands. His face was blotched and wet and ten years older than it had been a week ago. "It started with debts. Marra's doctors, at the end. You were at the abbey all day then, and too young to know how much, and I paid on them for years after. Thale bought them up, all of them, and then he came to me and said he'd forgive the lot, and all I had to do was sign a loss when he told me there'd been a loss. That's all. Sign my name. The ships weren't even really lost, he said; the crews were paid off and went home, nobody drowned, the only one who lost anything was the Crown, and the Crown's a thief anyway." He laughed, horribly. "And it was true. That was the worst of it. For three years it was true. Nobody drowned."

"Until Mallory."

"Until Idris." He looked down at the drawer on the floor. "He came to me the night before. After he'd been in here. He said, *Orrin, I've found it, and I'm taking it to Pellmouth, and I'm giving you one day to come with me and tell them yourself, because I'd rather it was you.* One day. And I went to Thale." His voice dropped to almost nothing. "I went to Thale that night, God forgive me. I thought — I thought he'd let me go. I thought if I told him first he'd let me go."

Tamsin thought of Mallory in the cold office with his hat on, telling her not to mention the *Heron* to her uncle, and understood for the first time that it had not been kindness to Orrin, or not only. He had been keeping Orrin for himself. He had wanted to give him his day, and he had not trusted her to let him have it.

The light was coming up grey in the window behind him. Out on the Mole a cart went by, early, its wheels loud on the cobbles.

"Where's the ledger?" Tamsin said.

He was silent.

"Uncle. They have Pell. He's twelve. Where is it?"

"If it leaves my keeping," Orrin said, "it leaves his. That's what he wrote. You read it." He looked up at her. "Do you know what that means? It means the day that book leaves this office, Thale has nothing left to lose. It's the only thing keeping me alive, Tamsin. It's the only thing keeping you alive."

"And Pell?"

He did not answer that. He got up, slowly, like an old man, and went to the wall behind the desk, and moved aside a chart of the Narrows — the soundings on it out of date by twenty years — and behind it, set into the stone, was a small iron door, no bigger than a book, with a keyhole in the middle of it shaped like a wave.

"The tide-key," he said, and took from round his neck a thing she had seen there every day of her life and never once thought about: a heavy brass key on a leather cord, the bow of it worked into the shape of a breaking wave. "Every harbourmaster since the charter has worn it. It's for the salt-book. It's the only thing it's for." He put it in the lock, and turned it, and the little door opened.

The ledger was inside. It was very ordinary. It was bound in brown calf and had *SALT* stamped on the spine in gilt that had nearly all worn off, and it was the dullest-looking book Tamsin had ever seen.

Her uncle did not take it out. He stood with his hand on the little iron door, and he said, without turning round:

"There's someone coming up the Mole."

scenes.title: Behind the chart
scenes.text:
It was Thale.

She knew his step before she saw him through the window. She did not know how; she had only heard it once, on the Lantern Stair. But there was something in it — unhurried, exact, a man who had never in his life had to walk faster than he wished. He was alone. He was carrying a cane he did not need.

"Hide," said Orrin.

"Where?"

He pointed. The lamp-room ladder went up through a trap in the ceiling, and Tamsin went up it so fast she barked both shins, and pulled the trap down behind her to within a finger's width of shut, and lay on the dusty boards of the old lamp-room with her eye to the gap.

She saw her uncle close the little iron door and turn the key and swing the chart back across it. She saw him pick up the warehouseman's book from the desk, and look round the room, wildly, and then shove it into the drawer that was lying on the floor and kick the drawer under the desk. Then he sat down, and put both hands flat on the tide-tables, and the door opened.

"Harbourmaster," said Corvan Thale. "You're early at your desk."

"So are you, magistrate."

"I've had a disturbed night." Thale came in, and shut the door behind him, and stood looking round the office with his cane under his arm, the way he had looked at Mallory on the Stair: patiently, regretfully, missing nothing. "Some property of mine was interfered with in the Quarter. A boy was taken up. Your niece's friend, I think — the little runner, with the nose."

"Pell," said Orrin.

"Pell. Yes." Thale took off his gloves, finger by finger. "A very loyal boy. He's told my sergeant nothing whatever, which is admirable in its way and very tiresome in all the others. But Ashcombe's boat was seen, and a woman was seen with her, and the woman went over the roofs like a cat with something under her arm." He laid the gloves on the corner of the desk, squared to the edge, the way Mallory had squared the letter; and Tamsin hated him for that more than for anything else. "I'd like it back, Orrin."

"I don't know what you mean."

"I think you do. I think it's very likely in this room." Thale's eyes went round the walls, the charts, the tide-tables, and stopped, for what seemed to Tamsin above him a very long time, on the chart of the Narrows. Then they moved on. "And I think, too, that it's very likely your niece is not far away. She's a clever girl. Idris trained her. Idris trained her very well." He smiled, a little. "I'd hate for her to be as clever as Idris. It ended so badly for him."

Orrin said nothing. Tamsin, above, could see the top of his head, the thinning place at the crown, and his hands on the desk had gone white at the knuckles.

"Here is what will happen," Thale said pleasantly. "Tonight is the big spring tide — the highest of the year. The Quarter will be under six feet. Very convenient, for a great many things. At the top of it, at the ninth bell of the evening, I shall be at the foot of the Lantern Stair, where poor Idris had his accident, with the boy. Your niece will bring me the warehouse book she took. You will bring me the other one, the one you keep for us. And the boy will go home to whoever owns him, and you and I, Orrin, will discuss your retirement." He picked up his gloves. "If she doesn't come — or if anyone comes but the two of you — then I'm afraid the steps at the bottom of the Stair are very slick at high water, and boys are so careless."

He went to the door. With his hand on the latch he paused.

"Oh — and the weather tonight is to be filthy. Tell her to wear a good coat." He looked up, for just a moment, directly at the trap in the ceiling, at the finger's-width of dark, and Tamsin, above him in the dust, did not breathe. "Good morning, harbourmaster."

The door closed behind him.

She lay on the boards of the lamp-room with her face in the dust and did not move until she heard his cane go away down the Mole, tap, tap, tap, as unhurried as a clock.

scenes.title: The lamp-room
scenes.text:
When she came down the ladder her uncle had not moved. He was sitting exactly as Thale had left him, with his hands flat on the desk, and he did not look round.

"He knew I was up there," Tamsin said.

"Yes."

"He looked right at me."

"He wanted you to know he knew. That's how he does it. He doesn't hide things, Tamsin, he shows you that he could have." Orrin turned his head at last. "Idris never understood that. Idris thought if you found the thing, you'd won. Thale doesn't care what you find. He cares what you can bear to do with it."

She went round the desk and knelt and pulled the drawer out from under it, and took the warehouseman's book out of it, and held it against her chest. Her uncle watched her do it and did not try to stop her.

"You'll come," she said. "Tonight. With the other one."

"I'll come."

"And after. When Pell's home. You'll come to Pellmouth with me, and tell the Assize what you told me. All of it. The debts, and Marra's doctors, and the nineteen ships."

He did not answer for a long time. Outside the gulls had started up along the Mole, the way they did when the fishing boats came in, a long ragged screaming that went on and on.

"Your aunt used to say," he said at last, "that I could never finish a thing I'd started. Not a fence, not a letter, not a pipe of tobacco. She said I'd leave my own funeral halfway through to see what the tide was doing." He almost smiled. "I'll finish this one. I promise you that."

It was not what she had asked. She knew it was not what she had asked. But he had put his hand out, across the tide-tables, and after a moment she took it, and it was warm and heavy and shaking very slightly, and they stayed like that in the grey office until the light was full and the first pilot came banging on the door for his chit.

scenes.title: The spring tide
scenes.text:
Thale had been right about the weather. By the afternoon the wind had gone round into the south-west and was blowing a full gale up the Narrows, and the sea was coming over the end of the Mole in long grey sheets, and the boats in the inner basin were snubbing at their moorings like dogs on chains. No ship would cross the bar in that. The Customs House sent its clerks home at three. Tamsin was not there to be sent; she was in the back room of the Gull and Lantern, in borrowed dry clothes that were too big for her, with Nessa Brack standing over her like a wall.

"You'll eat that," Nessa said, of a bowl of stew. "You'll eat it all. I don't care if you're sick after. I'll not have you going out in that on nothing."

"Nessa, I can't —"

"You can." Nessa sat down across from her, which was a thing Tamsin had never seen her do in four years of drinking in the Gull. "Bel Ashcombe came in last night at two in the morning, bleeding from the head, and told me what happened. Then she went out again before I could stop her. She said to tell you she's not dead and she's not running." Nessa's red face was set. "I said I'd tell you. I didn't say I'd agree with it."

Tamsin put down her spoon. "Where did she go?"

"To the *Merrow*. Where else does that woman ever go?" Nessa leaned forward. "Listen to me, girl. I've kept this house twenty-two years. I've seen Corvan Thale come up from a court clerk to the bench, and I've seen what happens to people who stand in his road, and none of it was weather. You go out on that Stair tonight and he'll have the book off you and the boy too, like as not, and then he'll have you." She sat back. "So you'll eat that stew."

Tamsin ate the stew.

When she had finished, Nessa took the bowl away and came back with something wrapped in oilcloth, and set it on the table. It was long and narrow and heavy.

"My Davey's," she said. "From when he was on the revenue cutters. It's not been fired since he died, but I've kept it oiled." She did not unwrap it. "I'm not saying you'll want it. I'm saying you'll have it."

Tamsin let the oilcloth lie there a long time, and then shook her head, and pushed it back across the table.

"I can't," she said. "I'd only drop it in the sea. Or shoot Pell." She tried to smile. "I find brandy, Nessa. I don't shoot people."

Nessa looked at her with an expression Tamsin couldn't read. Then she took the oilcloth bundle away, and did not argue.

"There's something you can do for me, though," Tamsin said, when Nessa came back. "Can you get word to the *Merrow* before dark?"

"I can get word anywhere before dark."

"Then tell Bel this. The top of the tide isn't at the ninth bell. It's at twenty past. Thale's reading the almanac, and the almanac's made for Pellmouth, and the Narrows hold the water back a quarter of an hour and more on a spring." She heard herself and it was the clerk's voice again, level, reading out a lading. "Tell her to lie off the end of the Mole with no lights showing. And tell her to come in when the lowest lantern on the Stair goes out. Not before."

Nessa was quiet for a long time. "And how," she said, "is the lowest lantern going to go out?"

"I'm going to put it out," said Tamsin.

At the door she took Mallory's hat out from inside her coat, where it had been since the Quarter, flattened and salt-stiff, and held it out. "Keep this for me."

Nessa took it in her red hands and turned it over, and looked at the torn brim, and did not ask. She hung it on the hook behind the bar, under the green lantern, and Tamsin buttoned the warehouseman's book inside her coat, where the hat had been.

There was a message waiting for her at the door when she left. It was from Sister Wren, and it had been written the day before and sent down to the Gull by the carrier's boy, because, Wren had written on the outside, everybody in Saltgate came into the Gull in the end, and it said, in Wren's tiny old upright script: *The copy I made at dinner has gone to the Assize at Pellmouth by the carrier, as he would have sent it. I am too old to be frightened of magistrates. You are not. Be careful. — W.*

She read it twice, standing in the doorway of the Gull with the gale screaming round the corner and the spray coming over the wall. Then she folded it small and put it in her boot, with the letter, where everything went. Then she went out into the gale.

scenes.title: The ninth bell
scenes.text:
The Lantern Stair at the top of the spring tide was a different place from the one she knew. The sea had come right up the face of the wall, higher than she had ever seen it, higher than any table she had copied said it could come, and of the hundred and twelve steps there were not more than seventy above the water, and the water itself was not water but a churning grey-white field that heaved and fell against the rock and threw itself up in fountains that broke over the lanterns on their brackets. Half the lanterns had gone out. The ones that were still lit swung in the wind and made the whole Stair seem to tilt.

Her uncle was waiting at the top. He had the salt ledger under his coat, wrapped in oilcloth; she could see the shape of it. He did not say anything when she came up. He only looked at her, and then at the book under her own arm — the warehouseman's book — and nodded once, and they went down together. Tamsin looked once at the end of the Mole as they went. There was nothing there. There was not meant to be.

Thale was at the bottom of what was left of the Stair, on the last step above the water, with the sea breaking at his feet. He had two men with him. One of them was the tall thin one with the bad teeth. The other was holding Pell by the collar, at arm's length, out over the water, the way you would hold a cat you meant to drown.

Pell's face was white and set and furious. He was not crying. When he saw Tamsin he shouted something, but the wind took it.

"Clerk Vey," said Thale. He had to raise his voice, and he did not seem to enjoy it. "Harbourmaster. Punctual. I do so appreciate it. The books, please."

"The boy first," said Tamsin.

"No," said Thale, quite kindly. "The books first. And then the boy. That is how this goes, I'm afraid. I'm the one who's holding something over the sea."

Orrin went down the last few steps. He went slowly, with his hand on the rail, and the spray soaked him, and when he was two steps above Thale he stopped and took the ledger out from under his coat and held it out, in its oilcloth.

Thale took it. He unwrapped it, there in the wind, and opened it, and read the first page, and the second, and smiled.

"Thank you, Orrin," he said. "Now Clerk Vey's."

"And the letter?" Tamsin said. She had not meant to say it. "Idris's letter. You haven't asked for it."

Thale smiled at her with the spray running off the brim of his hat. "Keep it, Clerk Vey. Keep it for Idris. I have never in my life sealed a letter whose first draft I did not keep, and the thing in your boot is a clerk's copy. Anyone can copy a hand. Ask your nun." He settled the ledger under his arm. "I'm told she's very good at it."

And Tamsin understood, standing on the step with the sea at her feet, that she had been carrying the wrong thing for five days. The letter had never been the danger to him. The danger was the place he kept the other one. Wren had seen that at a window in the abbey with the paper held to her nose, and had sent her copy to Pellmouth not as proof but as a question, to the one court in the kingdom that could make him answer it.

Tamsin did not move.

"Clerk Vey," said Thale. "The boy is getting heavy for Sergeant Marsh."

She went down. She was not calm. She was counting. She could feel the tide in the step under her feet the way she could feel a wrong figure in a column before she found it, and it was not at the top yet; it was still coming. She went down past her uncle, and as she passed the lowest lantern still burning she put out her hand to its bracket, as if to steady herself, and lifted the lantern off its hook and let it fall. It went into the sea without a sound that anyone could hear. Nobody looked at it. Half the lanterns on the Stair had gone out already.

Then she held out the warehouseman's book, and Thale took it from her with his free hand, and nodded to the sergeant, and the sergeant swung Pell back in over the steps and let go of him, and Pell fell against Tamsin's legs and clung there.

"There," said Thale. "Now. Was that so —"

The *Merrow* came round the end of the Mole.

She came with every rag of sail she owned set and drawing, in a gale that would have had any sane master hove-to under bare poles, heeled so far over that her lee rail was under, and she came straight for the foot of the Lantern Stair as if she meant to put her bowsprit through the sea-wall. Tamsin had one glimpse of Bel at the tiller, hatless, with her hair streaming and her mouth open in what might have been a shout or a laugh — and then the lugger's bow came up on a wave, high, impossibly high, level with the step they were standing on.

Everybody moved at once.

The tall man with the bad teeth went backward up the steps, fast. The sergeant let go of everything and threw himself flat. Thale — Thale did not move at all. He stood on the last step with both books in his arms and stared at the lugger rising out of the sea at him, and for the first time since Tamsin had known him his long clever face was simply, entirely blank.

And Orrin Hask came down the last two steps and put both arms round him, round him and the books together, the way he had once put his arms round Tamsin on the step of the Customs House on her first day, and stepped off the Stair with him into the sea.

Tamsin did not scream. She remembered that afterwards, and was ashamed of it, and later was not. She stood on the step with Pell holding her legs and watched the place where the water had closed, and the *Merrow*'s bow came down on it and rose again, and there was nothing there, and she went on watching it until Bel's hand closed on her arm and somebody lifted Pell away from her, and she understood that she was going to have to climb the Stair now, one step at a time, and that there were seventy of them.

scenes.title: Morning
scenes.text:
They found Thale at low water, at the bottom of the Stair, wedged among the rocks on the ninth step below the last, where they had found Mallory. He was alive. He had a broken leg and three broken ribs and had swallowed a great deal of the harbour, and for a day nobody was sure he would keep living, and then it became clear that he would, and he was carried up to the cells under his own court to wait for the men from Pellmouth.

They found the ledger the same morning, a little further along the rocks, still in its oilcloth. The warehouseman's book was gone. It did not matter. The Assize men, when they came two days later in a closed carriage with a letter from the Crown's own justiciary, had Wren's fair copy, and asked for the original in the place Wren's covering note named: a press in the magistrate's own chambers, where Corvan Thale had filed, in a letter-book bound in black, the first draft of every letter he had ever sealed, dated and very neatly kept. Idris's letter was in it under the eighth, in the fine joined hand. The letter Thale had not thought worth asking for on the Stair was a copy; the book that hanged him was his own. They had that, and the salt ledger, and Bel Ashcombe, who stood up in the court with her gold earring and her terrible coat and said exactly what she had done and who had paid her to do it and asked, quite politely, to be fined.

It came out at the Assize, too, why the men breaking the *Heron* had put down their saw in the middle of a stroke: word had come down from the court on the night of the tenth that the Customs House had an assessor asking questions, and they were to leave her where she lay until the questions stopped.

They did not find Orrin.

The sea kept him. Nessa said it often did that, with the ones it wanted, and that he would come ashore at Carrow or on the Tithes in a month or so, and that Tamsin should not go and look. Tamsin went and looked anyway, every low water for a week, along the foot of the sea-wall with Pell trailing after her picking up shells. She found a great many things — a boot, a bottle, a child's wooden horse, the brass tide-key on its leather cord, caught on a spur of rock under the Lantern Stair — and she did not find him.

She kept the key. She did not know what else to do with it. She wore it round her neck under her shirt, where it lay cold against her breastbone, and on the eighth morning, when she went back to work at the Customs House for the first time since Mallory, she found that somebody had hung his hat — cleaned, and the torn brim stitched — on the peg behind his desk in the narrow cold office at the seaward end of the building, as if he had only stepped out.

There was a new assessor coming from Pellmouth. Until he came, Fennick said, somebody had to sign the books.

Tamsin sat down at Mallory's desk, and lit the stove, and opened the tide-book.
